question: Do the flaps' phonetic environments group into communities, and do those communities line up with underlying /t/ versus /d/?

failed_criteria.statement: Best WavJEPA layer beats the MFCC baseline
failed_criteria.threshold: gap >= 0.05 balanced accuracy, and paired word-type bootstrap 95% lower bound > 0
failed_criteria.result: best layer 3: 0.5438; MFCC 0.5274; gap +0.0163 (needs >= 0.05); paired word-type bootstrap 95% CI [-0.0154, +0.0561] (lower bound needs > 0)

findings.statement: 25.1% of joint test sites (2,612) have their lemma in training with the same label; the split is disjoint by word form, not lemma. On the 7,586 lemma-unseen sites the gap to MFCC is +0.030, CI [-0.004, +0.073], still short of criterion 1.
The gap to MFCC's paired word-type bootstrap interval is [-0.015, +0.056]: no evidence of an advantage over MFCC, which is not evidence of none.

findings.cause: Sites aren't what the inventory says
findings.status: ruled out for the sites, not the labels
findings.statement: A blind listening audit of 80 sites heard a flap in 72 of 74 decidable cases (6 /d/ can't-tells), and the right word and a well-placed clip in all 80. The labels come from the dictionary form and can't be heard under a flap, so the audit clears the sites, not the labels.
Retraining the single-axis conditions at joint's training size (about 64% of sites) costs 0.006–0.013 at the best layer, against a 0.108 drop from random to joint.

Sites are 2–4 encoder frames wide (median 3, 27.4 ms). For MFCC, whose 25 ms frames see only local audio (deltas reach ±40 ms), a cue outside those frames, such as the preceding vowel's length, is invisible to the probe. WavJEPA encodes the flap ± 200 ms as one excerpt, so at depth its flap frames can carry that context; for WavJEPA the pilot shows only that the cue wasn't linearly recoverable from those frames. Untested: the span grid, registered 2026-10-17, tests both.
evidenced_by: Environment env-v-flap-v (status: planned) - The preceding stretch through the following segment.

findings.cause: The cue doesn't generalize to unseen words
findings.statement: The drop from random to joint is mostly the word axis: holding out speakers costs little, holding out word types costs most of the gap above chance.

answer:
**Yes, the environments form communities, but they only partly line up with /t/ versus /d/.** The rows don't say how the community graph was built or whether the modularity was tested against a null.

**Grouping.** Phones partition into 18 communities with modularity 0.4706, a moderate level of structure [community:1]. Sizes range from 1,804 sites [community:1] down to 15 [community:17] [community:18].

**Alignment with /t/ vs /d/.** Overall, 24.32% of sites are /d/. Most communities sit near that rate:

- [community:3] 0.26
- [community:4] 0.24
- [community:5] 0.20
- [community:8] 0.29

A few large communities depart clearly:

- [community:7] (n, en, s, z, k, g and others) is 57.2% /d/, the only sizeable /d/-majority group [community:7].
- [community:2] is only 6.3% /d/ across 1,630 sites [community:2].
- [community:9] (12.4%) [community:9] and [community:10] (11.4%) [community:10] lean /t/.

The other departures are tiny. /r/ is 51% /d/ on 37 sites [community:15], and /em/ is 0% on 15 sites [community:18]. No community is close to label-pure, and /t/ is the majority in all but two.

**Caveat.** The /t/–/d/ labels come from the dictionary form, not from what is heard. The listening audit cleared the sites, not the labels [find-sites].

**Missing.** To say whether these skews exceed chance or follow word identity, I'd need a significance test or a breakdown by word type.
